The Watchlist: April 2026
By Tobias Carroll
Tobias Carroll returns with new recommendations for your TBR list: Urdu poetry, novels from Brazil and India, Sámi folktales, and more.
April 27, 2026
Brazil India Norway South Korea Spain Reading Lists
From Black Ocean | Lightmesh by Choi Jeongrye, translated from the Korean by Sue Hyon Bae and Mattho Mandersloot | Poetry | 104 pages | ISBN 9781965154175 | US$18.00
What the publisher says: “ Lightmesh , Choi Jeongrye’s final book, performs a dislocation of the everyday. In poems that are playful, imaginative, and sometimes surreal, we move through a series of familiar yet uncanny locations, always grounded with Choi’s wit. This book showcases Choi’s style with succinct imagery and descriptions of everyday life in deceptively simple language.”
What Eun-Gwi Chung says: “Reading Choi’s poetry, which freely traverses the boundaries of prose and verse, readers are drawn into a flexible flow of time and space, blurring the lines between reality and dream, between prose and poetry. Her poems move like consciousness itself—associative, nonlinear, embracing contradiction.”
What I say: In one of the introductory texts for this collection, readers will find a quote from Choi Jeongrye: “I wanted to write poems that question origins, how to get in and how to get out . . .” That sense of destabilization is present throughout the book, sometimes literally. Take these lines from “Sesame Sprouts”: “My hair wasn’t attached to my skin / I think it just drifted through the air,” for instance. It’s a powerful collection, and one that I hope will lead to the translation of Choi’s earlier books as well.
From Transit Books | The Abyss by Jeyamohan, translated from the Tamil by Suchitra Ramachandran | Fiction | 352 pages | ISBN 9798893380040 | US$26.95
What the publisher says: “Pothivelu Pandaram is known as a successful, God-fearing man about town: He has a loyal wife, three daughters, and money to pay for their dowries. However, it’s an open secret that his success is fueled by a trade that is as profitable as it is cruel: He owns—and breeds—a group of physically deformed beggars and places them outside temples to collect money.”
What Publishers Weekly says: “Originally published in 2003, this deeply human story from Jeyamohan ( Stories of the True ) tells of slavery, religious hypocrisy, official corruption, and arranged marriage in 1991 Tamil Nadu. [. . .] [T]he novel is eminently readable, thanks to the unsparing view not just of Pandaram’s cruelty but his folly, as well as the wit and wisdom of the beggars.”
What I say: This is a disquieting novel from the outset, one in which familiar-seeming family bonds are revisited with troubling power dynamics, and accompanied by case studies in sincerity and hypocrisy. The prospect of a wedding at the center of a story is a time-honored literary tradition; in this context, though, it’s disturbing, and indicative of how this novel distorts common tropes. Also worth mentioning: The Translator’s Note left me with a lot of insight into the author’s use of language in the original, and with an inkling to read more books by Jeyamohan.
From University of Wisconsin Press | Sleep Journeys by Azra Abbas , translated from the Urdu by Daisy Rockwell | Poetry | 144 pages | ISBN 9780299355647 | US$18.95
What the publisher says: “A single book-length poem, divided into three cantos, Sleep Journeys is a dreamlike rumination that explores faith, female desire, and the subconscious mind. Abbas’s language is simple and austere, the complexity of the work emerging through repetition, interweaving, and juxtaposition.”
What translator Daisy Rockwell says: “ Sleep Journeys reminded me that translation is above all an act of blind faith. We translators have no way of knowing if we’ll succeed, what that success would look like, how the text will manifest rewoven in a new language, and how it will be experienced by new readers. Every translation is a journey, but this translation was for me a mystical voyage.”
What I say: Daisy Rockwell’s translation of Abbas’s collection into English abounds with evocative and detailed images, such as this: “Pillows placed on empty beds recline like sad girls.” As the dreamlike state suggested by the title promises, the scenes contained within are free-flowing and allusive, with qualities both ephemeral and tactile.
From University of Minnesota Press | Sámi Folktales from the Near and Far Worlds , collected by Just Knud Qvigstad and Isak Saba, translated from the Norwegian by Barbara Sjoholm | Folktales | 480 pages | 9781517916749 | US$39.95
What the publisher says: “Originally recorded in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries by the Norwegian philologist Just Knud Qvigstad and the Sámi politician and folklorist Isak Saba, this collection spans centuries of storytelling in multiple genres, from migratory fairy tales with kings and princesses to legends of ghosts and the Devil to fables with talking animals.”
What Elin Anna Labba says: “For decades, these stories have provided contemporary Sámi literature with drama, detail, and inspiration. This collection is a treasure trove for every writer and reader to explore, and it’s a gift to the English language that these folktales are now translated.”
What I say: This is a wide-ranging collection of stories, covering a lot of ground. Some of these tales contain explicitly Christian messages. Others are stranger, including one where a plague can be killed with a gunshot, and another where a human and a bear make a mutual castration pact. Musicians, take note: The title of 90% of the stories in the “Omens and Hauntings” section would make for excellent doom metal song titles, including “Green Flame on the Sea” and “Those Who Lie in Wait for Furbearers Often See Ghosts.”
From Foreshore Books | Springtime in the Bones by Állex Leilla, translated from the Portuguese by Amanda Sarasien | Fiction | 240 pages | ISBN 9781919252681 | UK£9.50
What the publisher says: “Set in Salvador, Bahia, the novel follows Luísa, a rising star in the advertising world—clever, stylish, admired. But beneath her polished exterior lies a woman piecing herself back together from two shattering blows: a violent rape and the collapse of a marriage she fought desperately to save.”
What Ilze Duarte at Reading in Translation says: “Luísa’s pursuit of revenge is likely to be disturbing to readers, as it was to me. But I hope they will appreciate, as I do, Állex Leilla’s decision to create a female character who doesn’t wither after the violence that is perpetrated against her, who refuses to be meek and intimidated.”
What I say: With rapid-fire prose, Állex Leilla narrates the aftermath of a horrific act and her protagonist’s quest for revenge. Several chapters are told entirely through dialogue, which contributes significantly to the sense of momentum here. The prose, in Amanda Sarasien’s translation, does as well: “The small hours can dream up what doesn’t exist and push you downhill.”
From Other Press | The Pain of Others by Miguel Ángel Hernández , translated from the Spanish by Adrian Nathan West | Fiction | 320 pages | ISBN 9781635424607 | US$18.99
What the publisher says: “In this blend of police thriller and poignant autofiction, a writer revisits a tragic crime from his adolescence and reckons with a dark, underexplored side of Spain. . . . Twenty years later, when the wounds seem to have stopped bleeding and the mourning died down, Miguel decides to return to the countryside and, putting himself in the shoes of a detective, tries to reconstruct that tragic night that marked the end of his adolescence.”
What Publishers Weekly says: “Spanish writer Hernández ( Anoxia ) chronicles in this searching autofiction his attempt to write a novel about his boyhood best friend, Nicolás, who killed his older sister, Rosi, when he was 18, before jumping off a cliff to his death. . . . Though Miguel doesn’t solve the mystery of Nicolás’s motive, he offers a weighty reflection on the repressed Catholic lowlands of his and Nicolás’s childhood . . .”
What I say: This haunting work of autofiction opens with what seems to be news of a kidnapping and murder, but which is revealed to be something even worse. The narrator is haunted by “the perplexity of the instant when Nicolás ceased to be my friend and became a monster.” If this was a straightforward work of memoir, it would be compelling enough, but as its narrator works his way through true crime tropes and the enduring attraction of terrible events, it becomes something even more powerful: an unforgettable meditation on memory and violence.
